I am 53 years old and have been farming these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man. I never went to school, but I know this land and I know what works. Every year I grow winter wheat and summer maize — that is what our land and our climate are made for here on the North China Plain. My father did it this way, my neighbors do it this way, and I will not change what has fed my family for generations.

I have about 7 mu of good flat land. In October I will sow wheat after rotary tilling the maize stubble. I use an improved wheat seed — something like Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22 — because the yield is steady and the grain buyer knows it. Before sowing I spread two bags of compound fertilizer per mu, and in the spring I topdress with one bag of urea when the wheat starts to shoot up. I irrigate three times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from the cold, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I spray herbicide once after sowing, insecticide twice when the aphids come, and fungicide once if the weather turns damp. I expect about 1,000 jin of wheat per mu.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I plant maize the same day or the next. I do not till — I sow directly into the wheat stubble. Everyone here uses Denghai 605; it is a hybrid seed and it gives me over 1,100 jin per mu if the rain and the irrigation come right. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and sometimes a little urea later if the leaves look yellow. Maize needs two irrigations: one when it is knee-high and one when the cobs are filling. I spray herbicide once and insecticide two or three times for the corn borer. I harvest in October, then the cycle starts again.

I do not grow cotton anymore. The cotton price goes up and down like a wild horse, and it needs too much spraying — twelve, thirteen times a season. My back is not what it used to be, and wheat and maize are reliable. The grain station buys them every year.
